passages.happening:
“Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God. For many false prophets have gone out into the world. By this you will know the Spirit of God: Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist, which you have heard is coming and which is already in the world at this time” (verses 1-3).

“You, little children, are from God and have overcome them, because greater is He who is in you than he who is in the world. They are of the world. That is why they speak from the world’s perspective, and the world listens to them. We are from God. Whoever knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. That is how we know the Spirit of truth and the spirit of deception” (verses 4-6).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 3 ended with the Spirit God has given. But many people claimed the Spirit, including those who had left. So John shows how to tell.

The early church valued prophecy as a gift of the Spirit, and travelling prophets were common. That made discernment urgent. In the wider Greek and Roman world, oracles and inspired speech were part of everyday religion. A claim to be moved by a spirit carried no automatic weight. John's readers knew that not every voice that sounded inspired came from God.

The word ‘test’ is the one used for testing metal to see if it was genuine. John's test is a confession: ‘Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.’ That points again to what the teachers who left were denying. They seem to have said that the divine Christ was not truly and lastingly joined to a human body. Early in the second century, Ignatius of Antioch wrote to churches in the same region, warning against teachers who said that Christ only seemed to suffer. John's letter shows the same danger at an earlier stage.

Then John steadies his readers. They have overcome the false teachers, not because they are clever, but because ‘greater is He who is in you than he who is in the world’. The false teachers are popular; ‘the world listens to them’. Being listened to is not proof of truth.

‘Whoever knows God listens to us.’ John speaks for the apostles and first witnesses. The test is whether people receive the apostolic message about Jesus.
passages.ot:
The law gave Israel a test for prophets too. A prophet who drew people to other gods was not to be followed, even if a sign came true: “you must not listen to the words of that prophet or dreamer” (Deuteronomy 13:3).

And Jeremiah warned of prophets who spoke their own minds: “The prophets are prophesying lies in My name,” and, “I did not send them or appoint them or speak to them” (Jeremiah 14:14).

The confidence that God is greater than every enemy is Israel's. When an army surrounded the prophet Elisha, he told his frightened servant that “those who are with us are more than those who are with them” (2 Kings 6:16).
passages.hard:
‘Test the spirits.’ How should Christians do that today, and does it mean being suspicious of everyone?

John's test is not suspicion. It is loyalty to the truth about Jesus. The first question to ask of any teacher or movement is what it says about Jesus Christ: is he the eternal Son of God who truly came in the flesh, died and rose? Paul gives a similar instruction: “Do not treat prophecies with contempt, but test all things. Hold fast to what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:20-21).

Christians apply this in different ways. Some churches expect prophecy and other gifts of the Spirit today and test them carefully against Scripture. Others hold that such gifts were for the founding of the church and test all teaching by the written word. All agree that no claim to the Spirit stands above the apostles' witness to Christ.

Testing is not the same as treating every person who disagrees with you as an enemy. John's test is about the truth of Christ, not about winning arguments over smaller questions.
passages.asks: Ask whose voices shape what you believe about God, and whether you have tested them. Ask what they say about Jesus Christ come in the flesh. And ask whether you are tempted to think that a popular message must be true.

passages.happening:
“Beloved, let us love one another, because love comes from God. Everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God. Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love” (verses 7-8).

“This is how God’s love was revealed among us: God sent His one and only Son into the world, so that we might live through Him. And love consists in this: not that we loved God, but that He loved us and sent His Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins” (verses 9-10).

“Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another. No one has ever seen God; but if we love one another, God remains in us, and His love is perfected in us” (verses 11-12).
passages.hearers:
This is one of the richest passages on love in the Bible. The word for love, in noun and verb, comes in nearly every sentence.

‘God is love.’ To ancient ears this was unusual. Greek stories told of gods who loved and lusted, but the gods were not love itself. Philosophers often pictured the highest god as unmoved and self-sufficient, not as one who sends his son to die. John does not say ‘love is God’, as if every kind of love were divine. He says ‘God is love’, and he at once shows what he means by pointing to what God did.

‘God sent His one and only Son.’ The phrase ‘one and only’ translates monogenēs, unique, one of a kind; it was used of an only child. Older translations said ‘only begotten’. Verse 9 reads almost like a comment on John 3:16.

Then verse 10 turns everything around. Love does not start with us. ‘Not that we loved God, but that He loved us.’ And it is measured by cost: he sent his Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins.

So, John says, ‘we also ought to love one another’. And he adds a striking thought. No one has seen God. But when believers love one another, God's love is ‘perfected’, made complete, in them. The unseen God becomes visible in a loving church.
passages.ot:
God's love is the heart of his name in the law: “The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6).

The prophets heard God speak of his love as older than any response from Israel: “I have loved you with an everlasting love; therefore I have drawn you with loving devotion” (Jeremiah 31:3).

And the law already said that God's love comes first: “The LORD did not set His affection on you and choose you because you were more numerous than the other peoples” but “because the LORD loved you” (Deuteronomy 7:7-8).
passages.asks: Ask what you think love is, and whether you have learned it from the cross. Ask what it means to you that God loved you before you loved him. And ask where, in your church or home, the unseen God could be seen this week in the way you love.

passages.happening:
“By this we know that we remain in Him, and He in us: He has given us of His Spirit. And we have seen and testify that the Father has sent His Son to be the Savior of the world. If anyone confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God” (verses 13-15).

“And we have come to know and believe the love that God has for us. God is love; whoever abides in love abides in God, and God in him” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Here John gathers the threads. How do we know we remain in God? Three things are named together. God has given us his Spirit. We confess that Jesus is the Son of God. And we abide in love.

‘We have seen and testify.’ John speaks again as one of the witnesses. What they saw was that ‘the Father has sent His Son to be the Savior of the world’. ‘The world’ here is all people, whom God loves.

‘We have come to know and believe the love that God has for us.’ Faith is not only believing facts about God. It is believing that he loves us.

Then John says it a second time: ‘God is love.’ And whoever lives in love lives in God. This is not a sentimental idea. In this letter love is defined by the cross and shown in open hands.
passages.ot:
Israel confessed God as the only Saviour: “I, yes I, am the LORD, and there is no Savior but Me” (Isaiah 43:11). John says that this God sent his Son ‘to be the Savior of the world’.

And the promise that God would live with his people runs through the law and the prophets: “And I will make My dwelling place among you, and My soul will not despise you. I will walk among you and be your God, and you will be My people” (Leviticus 26:11-12).
passages.asks: Ask whether you believe, not only that God exists, but that he loves you. Ask what it means for you to ‘abide in love’ today. And ask whom you could tell about the Saviour of the world.

passages.happening:
“In this way, love has been perfected among us, so that we may have confidence on the day of judgment; for in this world we are just like Him. There is no fear in love, but perfect love drives out fear, because fear involves punishment. The one who fears has not been perfected in love. We love because He first loved us” (verses 17-19).

“If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ but hates his brother, he is a liar. For anyone who does not love his brother, whom he has seen, cannot love God, whom he has not seen. And we have this commandment from Him: Whoever loves God must love his brother as well” (verses 20-21).
passages.hearers:
John now speaks of the day of judgment. He does not say it will not come. He says believers can face it with confidence.

Why? Because ‘love has been perfected among us’. God's love, received and returned, takes away the dread of punishment. ‘There is no fear in love.’ John is speaking of a particular fear: the fear that God is waiting to punish us. Those who know his love in the Son need not live under that.

Then four short words that sum up the letter: ‘We love because He first loved us.’

And the last test is sharp. A person who says ‘I love God’ and hates his brother is lying. It is easy to claim love for a God no one can see. The test is the brother or sister in front of you, whom you can see, and who may be hard to love.
passages.ot:
The law joined the two great commands. Love for God: “And you shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength” (Deuteronomy 6:5). Love for neighbour: “love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18).

And the psalms speak of confidence before God that rests on his mercy: “If You, O LORD, kept track of iniquities, then who, O Lord, could stand? But with You there is forgiveness, so that You may be feared” (Psalm 130:3-4).
passages.hard:
If God is love, how can he also judge? And what does it mean that ‘perfect love drives out fear’?

Some readers take ‘God is love’ to mean that a loving God could never condemn anyone. The tension is real. But the same chapter that says God is love also speaks of the day of judgment (verse 17) and of a sacrifice for sins (verse 10), which shows that sin is serious enough to need one. Most Christian teaching has held that God's love and his justice are not rivals. Love that did not oppose what destroys the beloved would be indifference, not love. The cross shows both at once: God does not overlook sin, and he bears its cost himself. Christians differ over how the final judgment works; the doctrine study on judgment sets out the views.

John's point here is pastoral. For those who have come to know God's love, judgment is no longer something to dread. Perfect love drives out fear because it rests on what God has done, not on how well we have loved.

This passage is not a rebuke of people who live with an anxiety disorder, panic attacks or depression. Those are real illnesses of body and mind, and they need care, not blame. Getting help is not a lack of faith, and nothing in this verse forbids it. A doctor, a counselor, medicine, one trusted person who will stay can all be part of how God cares for you. The Honest Answer ‘Is my anxiety a spiritual failure?’ says more. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask what you fear when you think of standing before God, and what this passage says to that fear. Ask who in your life is hard to love, and what it would mean to love them because God first loved you. And ask whether your love for God can be seen in how you treat your brother or sister.
